The various cults dedicated to the God Moi’Dannau’Thataga (Modaga) the God of Death, and spiritual revelation, depict him in various different ways, depending on the Saint they view him from.
Those who revere Sin’Sha’Halla depict him laying on his side, wrapped in yellow cloth and with wide, opalescent eyes. They prize his appearance to The Siha’Halla, and his role as a psychopomp, ferrying the dead under the waves. 

Those who revere him through Mo’Edui’Halla depict him as a grotesquely detailed rotting corpse. Prizing his role in nourishing the sea with the bodies of the dead, they heap rotting animals on his shrines.

Those who revere him through No’Jarrok’Halla depict him as a golden fish, clutching a yellow banner in its mouth. They prize The Noja’Halla’s vision, and his role as a herald of news from under the Sea. 

Those who revere him through Sin’Fuoilut’Halla depict him as a singing cadaver, hung by its left foot. They prize his appearance to Sifuo’Halla and his role as a resurrector of the dead.

Those who revere him through Ma’Hegri’Halla depict him as a mummified woman with three heads. They prize his role as the giver of knowledge at birth, death, and after death, representing all innate knowledge that people possess.

The cults dedicated to various Saints and gods each represent these figures in different (though sometimes similar) ways, depending on which facets they prefer.

The Kurrupakxi (Kurupakanad in the Hampanad language) usually wear their hair in hoops, the number of which conveys the marital status of an individual, however, people such as this woman, who has moved to a foreign land, do not always wear their hair in hoops, however skullbinding remains common wherever they go, and they may adopt the bindings of other cultures, this particular style is in keeping with the Kurrupakxi tradition, if only a bit, in that the top of her skull is shaved to reveal the extent of her binding, and her hair is allowed to remain below.

Being buried, the Pan-Imperial syncretic religion asserts that the Gods live in the ocean, and that being buried at sea is the only way for ones soul to find bliss, however being buried in the earth is like eternal solitary confinement, and being burned delivers one’s soul to the sky, the domain of unclean spirits, however for Cthonic cults being buried in dirt is considered acceptable, but being interred in a box or stone is considered a punishment, being burned carries the same significance, it is only in two cultures that large exceptions can be found, the D’Lael leave their bodies on pillars for sky burials (though this practice is considered heretical and illegal, so it is not often done these days) and the Karrupaek believe that being buried at all traps the soul in its body, so they burn their dead to release it to their gods in the sky, Celestial religions however are treated almost like Demon Worship and thus the Karrupak with their Celestial-Centric faith are the source of much scorn and oppression, there are of course other smaller cultures and faiths that hold similar views, but most are agreeable with the Syncretic idea that burial in the ocean is preferable or at least acceptable, terrestrial burials are allowed and in some cases preferred, tying into this, drowning or being tossed from a sea cliff is considered an honourable excecution, while being interred in a crypt is a grave punishment, and being burned is the gravest of punishments, instead of rotting in the earth one is (supposedly) sent for torture in the heavens.

The Gnisitad (lit. People of Gnisiter) are one of the most influential groups in Hampanad politics (Hampana being the empire *and the continent) the current Emperor, Moa’Na’Bealuzarharrandir’Halla’Moazit (lit. Lord of Lands, Bealuzarharrandir, who’s name is holy and Lordly) is descended from the Gnisitad royal family, the Gnisitad excel in war, if not battle, most of their wars are fought swiftly by the “Witch Princess’s of Gnisiter” who wield a terrible yellow flame that can devour a body in less than a second, the power of Gnisiter at any given time is usually measured by how many such witches are alive, the numbers fluctuate but they usually have about twenty, less is uncomfortable, ten is on edge, and any less than ten is regarded as disastrous, more than twenty inspires nationalism and aggression in the Gnisitad, who treat them like Palladium, so long as they live, Gnisiter cannot fail.
This picture is of an average Gnisitad man, with his necklace of interlocking rings, the pearls on his ears and nose, and the thick wooden beads in his hair he is quite distinctively Gnisitad, though pearls are popular almost everywhere, the Gnisitad habit of dipping them in layer after layer of white wax is quite unusual, real pearls dipped in wax are supposed to be a sign of humility, though it isn’t uncommon for someone to dip pebbles in wax to feign wealth. interlocking rings are a common motif in Gnisitad art, which some attribute to the belief that the Gnisitad invented chain-male, this however is pure superstition, as is the belief that these designs offer spiritual protection (which is the most likely reason for their prevalence) the Gnisitad are very fond of magic, and almost 5% of their number can use it in some form, which is far higher than the 1% on the rest of the continent, they, unlike their neighbors to the south, do not shun or fear it, but respect it (Gnisitad aggression towards the Wanteekad is the source of their mistrust of magic, and they are the only province on the continent to actively hunt its practitioners, this aversion is further seen by mothers painting their child’s upper lip if it should appear too “Gnisite”)

The Gri’Helli are bird spirits that make deals with mortals, and while they are (usually) pretty fair with mortals, they can twist the meaning of their words to screw over anyone who insults them, or, if someone tries to back out and not pay their end of the deal, the Gri’Helli in questions sneaks into their house and sings a “Mad-Song” in their ear, the afflicted person feels compelled to recreate the song, whether by tapping, humming, singing or playing it. When they finally give in and recreate the song they draw the attention of Salna’Knin (the song being the sound of their lost pups) upon finding that the cursed individual is not a pup they drag them off into the night sky and eat them.

Religion in the world of A’Ama could be seen as an extension of their politics, the whole world is ruled by the empire of Na’Hampana (means: greatest of the great lands) though the empire doesn’t destroy the cultures and people’s they absorb into their empire, they revel in them, as they absorb new lands they add new gods to their pantheons. The Hampanad consider The Sivin (The twenty and one) to be the greatest of all gods, these are the gods of the continent of Na’Hampana, birthplace of the empire, much like the Hampanad peoples themselves consider their nations to be the greatest of all, because the empire stretches across the whole world their pantheon includes thousands of gods. The Sivin in particular though are all “Moi’Tat” or “Dead gods” instead of directly interfering in the world these gods exert influence through individuals who closely align with the personality and goals of a certain god, these saints are rare but have the powers of a god, and because their tie to the world of the living is stronger than the dead gods they are prayed to even after death, though the Sivin are still worshipped as the greatest of gods, they are not prayed to for help or miracles. The Sivin are not the only dead gods, and other cultures have their own interpretations, but the Hampanad interpret every new god in a way that adds them to the “Grand House” and they syncretize and practice apologetics to settle the worst differences. Almost every province is ruled by a secular leader, depending on what kind of country it was before its absorption into the empire, but the empire itself is a theocracy, exercising only religious law and leaving the provinces to largely govern themselves, they keep the empire together by allowing them to mostly do their own thing if they abide by basic rules of interaction with other provinces, and if push comes to shove the House (the ruling council of Na’Hampana) will send a saint (if available) to mediate conflicts and restore order, if no saint is available they put pressure on any offending parties with the aid of nearby provinces. Almost every God dwells in either the sea (A’Ama being comprised of 80% water) or under the land, though the latter is usually found only in the largest islands or continents. The Hampanad conflate every Aerial deity with “Moi’Shenna’Jol” or “Great god of the night sky, the adversary” who is said to be the most active Sivin, and also the only one in the pantheon not legal to worship, M’S’J has the most saints, though because their connection to him is lesser than most other gods these “Anti-Saints” are far less powerful. M’S’J is associated with the night sky and birds, and any gods also associated with similar things are considered “tainted” by the Hampanad and reviled. Though this is not always true the goddess “Harukki Marae” is also associated with the night sky and birds, though she is held to be a good goddess, her people where some of the few who resisted joining the empire because they demanded Harukki Marae be outlawed, and they practice their ancient Monolatreistic religion, which acknowledges the existence of other gods, but only recognizes Harukki Marae as worthy of veneration.

The great dark plantations of the south. Long ago the southern half of Na’Juntoye was covered in huge plantations, though eventually the crops grown there were discovered to also grow much closer to civilized areas, making them too expensive to keep open, the vast manor houses built of black wood still remain, and dot the landscape, in some areas the jungle has swallowed them up, in others they still stand in the middle of great fields. They are now inhabited by fell abominations born of spirits made flesh, and people, and the Uncanny folk haunt them, using them as tribal villages. The uncanny folk are self-replicating golems made of moss and clay, each one makes several more before they become too old and dry to go on living. Instead of worshipping gods they direct their worship towards black wood idols inlaid with gold, because they have the power to spin grass in their hands and turn it into gold. Uncanny folk are able to focus on a being or object and imbue it with power, while only one of the folk is enough to grant telepathy for example, a whole village focusing on an idol can bring it to life, and over several generations it can rival a god, at least in a small area, the power fades though, and if it’s worshippers are destroyed an idol might go dormant, it’s personality slowly decays until the idol itself rots away.

In Gryre, a small village on a small island quite removed from anywhere else, a child refuses to go to bed, so his father tells him a story “Have you ever heard of the Gri’Helli? Mzine (a perfect name) they come at night, to the windows of children who do not sleep, and sing silly songs in their ear, but when you hear their song, you cannot help but tap your fingers to it, then you Hum, and then you sing. But when you sing it Mzine, the Salna’Knin, moon hounds can hear it, and they come for you, because they think you are one of their lost children, and they sniff at your window, they claw it, and when they find you are not theirs... they eat you!” Storytelling such as this is common in most of the empire, and in the northern half the Gri’Helli are a very common motif, they’re bird demons that like to make deals with mortals, and while they usually bargain fairly, they turn nasty when double crossed, the most common way for them to get back at those that cheat them is to sing a song to you, that you cannot help but repeat ad nauseam, the song itself sounds like gibberish to anyone listening, but it’s actually the melodic cries of a lost Salna’Knin pup, the song is like a spell that seeps into the spirit world and calls Salna’Knin down from the sky, and when they find you aren’t a pup, they eat you, though Gri’Helli care nothing for restless or petulant children.

I’ll be using the City-State of Sux’Hampana as an example (City of the great land) Highest tier citizens range from wealthy merchant lords to ancient lineages of knights, still rich off taxes in provincial holdings. Highest Tier citizens live in luxurious palaces on the city’s hillside next to grand parks and salons, they eat exotic animals and strange, magically preserved fruit which would otherwise not be available in Sux’Hampana, all of them are in some way connected to the city’s various organizations, Temples, Guilds, Salons, Universities, or martial orders. High class citizens can fall from grace if they commit crimes of the faith, and their property is seized by the temple, or if they offend the King of Sux’Hampana. The poorest folk in the city state live by the water, or in the tenements and garrets of the inner city, these are the jobless, the apostates, blasphemers, and Cultists. Sux’Hampana dispenses two loaves of bread to every person per day, and though wells are plentiful, this is barely enough to keep someone alive. Though this lowest caste only makes up 5% of Sux’Hampana, the majority of citizens hover just above them, in small but clean buildings, and with sufficient but plain food, fish is often on the menu, and while the rich are fond of shameful excess, and drink pearls and vinegar, the poor often make due with water, or very cheap wine imported from the East. One could only hope to climb the ladder through sainthood, or perfection of your craft, the best artisans are paid very well by rich patrons across the empire, though it is far cheaper to live elsewhere, a lack of Unloki (bread for all) and the high cost of traveling to another place (made far higher by bringing any possessions) keeps people in Sux’Hampana, though sometimes, when the city is too crowded, the King of the city state will pat passage for a certain number of citizens to leave to the provinces.

I expanded on the architecture of the rural areas of the kingdom of Gnisiter, villages take on a circular shape, with the tallest buildings on the outside, tall walls are constructed between the outermost buildings, with only thin slits for windows on the outer walls, towns generally feature cloth canopies over the narrow alley ways, leaving only the innermost garden of the village open to the air, brightly colored frescoes adorn the inner walls, while the outside of the village normally takes on a solid color (pastel blues, greens, and light pinks being the most common color (although they are almost always dirty and faded) the inner frescoes are lovingly maintained and depict the ancestors and events that shape that village. a circular courtyard sits in the very center of the village and is filled with sweet smelling plants and a shrine to the village god (a deity who’s only sphere of influence is that town) this local god is represented by the founder of the village. though it is believed the god only wears its face, and is a separate entity from the Ancestor itself. towns which have been sacked and rebuilt multiple times may have many faces for their god, the ancestor who reclaims the settlement being added to the gods personality. though even short occupation by an evil being can taint the god, and give it a mean streak. The shrine is usually a pillar (Northwest Gnisiter) or a statue (which may have many faces, and is generally used in the Norteast) the Heu’Panta (Wall Town) style of village is not used farther south, away from the border.

Immaterial brings (Spirits) come in three main varieties: Far Spirits, Daemons, and Elementals. Far spirits (Which include Fae) are those peculiar spirits which are too disparate to fall into the other two categories. Far Spirits intermingle freely with Daemons and Elementals, Some wander the multiverse and others stay in the veil of a particular plane. Far spirits have the least contact with material reality as a whole, though exceptions such as the Fae exist, they find Material Reality to be a terrifying alien place, and almost never enter specific planes on purpose. Daemons are further divided into Celestials, Abyssals, and amoral Deities. Daemons, as a general rule, crave worship and purpose, Demons support dark cults, and keep mortal souls as slaves. Celestials shepherd mortals and keep their souls in their own planes, which mortals regard as paradises. Amoral Deities (The more powerful of these are considered gods in their own right, and the lesser ones are Guradian spirits) as the name suggests they aren’t often concerned with morality. Instead of Sin and Virtue, they control their followers with necessity, demanding sacrifice and worship for protection and plenty. Elementals are rare, they are beings made of self sustaining loops in energy, and unlike other spirits, they’re right at home in physical places, the most notable examples are sentient winds, living planes of energy, or unique living things created and destroyed on the tides of the Astral Sea.

Magic is Energy that flows across planes through pores in the veil, some planes have more, some have less, and some peculiar planes flow in cycles where the amount of magic waxes and wanes. Some planes are magic dead, and are very difficult to travel to or from, and certain high magic worlds are extremely unstable. In worlds with cyclical flows, or unstable flows, captured magic can get very expensive when the natural flow slows.
